items: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). The direction matters.
Bayes with counts: 10,000 cases, split by the truth, then by the signal.
Answer = true positives / all positives.
The bottom of the fraction adds every group: the law of total probability.
A rare truth and an imperfect test give mostly false alarms.

lessons.title: Which distribution
lessons.intro: When a question counts something (how many succeed, how many arrive, which try is the first to work), a named distribution gives the answer in one line. The skill is to recognize which one.

blocks.html:
Which one

The question describesDistributionP(X=k)Mean
n independent tries, each with chance p. Count the successes.Binomial(nk)pk(1−p)n−knp
Draw n without replacement from N items, K of them special. Count the special ones.Hypergeometric(Kk)(N−Kn−k)(Nn)nK/N
Events arrive at an average rate λ per interval. Count the events.Poissone−λλkk!λ
Repeat a try with chance p until the first success. Count the tries.Geometric(1−p)k−1p1/p

Binomial

Worked example. Ten emails go out, and each is opened with probability 0.3.

Exactly 2 opened: (102)×0.32×0.78=45×0.09×0.0576=0.233.

At most 1 opened: 0.710+10×0.3×0.79=0.028+0.121=0.149.

At least 2 opened: 1−0.149=0.851.

"At least k" is 1 minus the cases below k. It is almost always the shorter route.

q.stem: A model is right on each case with probability 0.8, independently. What is the probability that it is right on exactly 4 of 5 cases? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain: Binomial with n=5 and p=0.8: (54)×0.84×0.2=5×0.4096×0.2=0.4096, which rounds to 0.410.

blocks.html:
Without replacement

When you draw from a small pool and don't put items back, each draw changes the odds, so the binomial is wrong. Count combinations instead.

Worked example. 20 invoices include 5 with errors. An auditor checks 4 at random.

Exactly 1 has an error: (51)(153)(204)=5×4554845=0.470.

None has an error: (154)(204)=13654845=0.282.

If the pool is huge compared with the sample, or items are put back, the draws are close to independent and the binomial is fine.

Poisson

Use it for counts of events in time or space when you are given an average rate. Scale the rate to the interval in the question first.

Worked example. A help desk gets 3 calls an hour on average.

Exactly 1 call in an hour: e−3×3=0.149. No call in an hour: e−3=0.050.

No call in 20 minutes: the rate for 20 minutes is 1, so e−1=0.368.

q.stem: A shop gets 4 orders an hour on average, and orders follow a Poisson distribution. What is the probability of no order in the next 30 minutes? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain: Scale the rate first: 4 an hour is 2 per 30 minutes. P(0)=e−2=0.135.

blocks.html:
First success

The first success comes on try k when the first k−1 tries fail and the next one works: (1−p)k−1p. No success in the first k tries: (1−p)k.

Worked example. Each sales call converts with probability 0.2. First sale on call 3: 0.82×0.2=0.128. No sale in the first 5 calls: 0.85=0.328. Calls needed on average: 1/0.2=5.

q.stem: A bag holds 8 good chips and 2 faulty ones. You take 3 without putting any back and count the faulty ones. Which distribution does the count follow?

options.text: Hypergeometric
options.why: A small pool and no replacement: each draw changes what is left.

options.text: Binomial with p = 0.2
options.why: The binomial needs the same chance on every draw. Here the chance changes after each chip.

options.text: Poisson
options.why: Poisson counts events that arrive at an average rate over an interval.

options.text: Geometric
options.why: Geometric counts the tries until the first success, not the successes in a fixed number of draws.

q.explain: Ask two questions. Is the number of tries fixed? Is the chance the same on every try? Fixed and the same: binomial. Fixed, but the pool shrinks: hypergeometric.

items: Fixed tries, same chance, independent: binomial.
Small pool, nothing put back: count combinations.
An average rate: Poisson. Scale the rate to the interval first.
"At least k" is 1 minus the cases below k.

lessons.title: Expected value, spread, and games with stages
lessons.intro: Some questions ask for an average outcome: the expected payoff, or the expected number of attempts. Others chain several steps, where each step depends on the one before. Both come down to weighting outcomes by their probabilities.

blocks.html:
Expected value

Multiply each outcome by its probability and add: E[X]=∑x·P(x).

Worked example. A promotion gives 50 points with probability 0.1 and 10 points with probability 0.3. Otherwise it gives nothing. The expected reward is 50×0.1+10×0.3=8 points.

Expected values add, even when the parts depend on each other: E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]. So 20 customers who each buy with probability 0.15 give 20×0.15=3 expected buyers, and you need no distribution to say so.

Expected number of tries

Add up the probability that each try happens at all. Try 1 always happens. Try 2 happens only if try 1 failed, and so on.

Worked example. A job is retried until it works, at most 4 times. Each try works with probability 0.5. Expected tries: 1+0.5+0.25+0.125=1.875.

With no limit on the number of tries, the sum comes to 1/p.

q.stem: You roll a fair die. A six pays 10 points, a four or a five pays 2 points, and anything else costs you 1 point. What is the expected payoff of one roll? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain: 10×16+2×26−1×36=116=1.833

blocks.html:
Variance and standard deviation

Variance measures spread: Var(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2. The standard deviation is its square root.

For independent quantities, variances add, and standard deviations don't:

  • A sum of n independent values, each with standard deviation σ, has standard deviation σn.
  • Their average has standard deviation σ/n.
  • A binomial count has variance np(1−p).

Worked example. 100 independent trials with p=0.2: the mean count is 20, the variance is 100×0.2×0.8=16, and the standard deviation is 4.

Covariance and correlation

Covariance says whether two quantities move together. Correlation is the covariance divided by both standard deviations, so it has no units and always lies between -1 and 1.

  • It measures straight-line association only. A perfect curve, such as y=x2 around zero, can have a correlation of 0.
  • Independent quantities have a correlation of 0. A correlation of 0 does not prove independence.
  • Changing the units, such as from meters to feet, leaves the correlation unchanged.

When two quantities are correlated, the variance of their sum gains a term:

Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)

q.stem: Daily sign-ups have a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 6, and the days are independent. What is the standard deviation of the total over 9 days?
q.explain:
Variances add: 9×62=324. The standard deviation is 324=18. The shortcut is 6×9.

Multiplying 6 by 9 is the common mistake. That would be right only if every day had the same value.

blocks.html:
Games with stages

When a question has steps, track what is left after each step. Multiply along a path, and add across paths. If the question says "at least one", work out the path where it never happens and subtract.

Worked example. A box holds 4 red and 6 blue balls. You draw 2. If both are blue, you set them aside and draw 2 more. What is the chance that you end up with at least one red ball?

The first draw is all blue: (62)/(102)=15/45=0.333.

The box now holds 4 red and 4 blue. The second draw is all blue: (42)/(82)=6/28=0.214.

No red at all: 0.333×0.214=0.071. At least one red: 1−0.071=0.929.

q.stem: You roll a fair die. If the result is below 4, you roll once more and keep the second result. Otherwise you keep the first result. What is the expected value of the number you keep?
q.explain:
Half the time the first roll is 4, 5, or 6, and you keep it. The average of those is 5. The other half you roll again, and a fresh roll averages 3.5.

0.5×5+0.5×3.5=4.25

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
first = rng.integers(1, 7, size=500_000)
second = rng.integers(1, 7, size=500_000)
kept = np.where(first < 4, second, first)

Expected tries: add the chance that each try happens. With no limit, 1/p.
Variances add for independent things. A sum of n has SD σ√n, and an average has σ/√n.
Correlation runs from -1 to 1 and sees straight lines only. Zero does not mean independent.
Staged game: track what is left after each step, and use the complement for "at least one".

lessons.intro: The other half of this module is statistics: where a value sits in a normal distribution, how precise an average is, and what an interval or a p-value does and doesn't say.

blocks.html:
Z-scores

A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: z=x−μσ.

Within 295%
Within 399.7%
Above +1, or below -116% each
Above +2, or below -22.5% each

Worked example. Test scores are normal with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10.

Above 90 is above z=2: 2.5%. Between 60 and 80 is within 1: 68%. Between 60 and 90 runs from z=−1 to z=2: 34% + 47.5% = 81.5%.

q.stem: Parcel weights are normal with a mean of 500 g and a standard deviation of 20 g. Using the 68-95-99.7 rule, what is the probability that a parcel weighs less than 460 g? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain: 460 g is 2 standard deviations below the mean. 95% of parcels lie within 2, which leaves 5% for the two tails, and half of that is below: 0.025.

blocks.html:
How precise is an average

An average from a sample has its own standard deviation, called the standard error. It shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so four times the data halves it.

SEmean=snSEproportion=p(1−p)n

Averages of many independent values are close to normal even when the raw data isn't. That is the central limit theorem, and it is why z-scores work for averages.

Confidence interval

estimate±z×SE

Use z=1.96 for 95%, 1.645 for 90%, and 2.576 for 99%.

Worked example. 100 orders have a mean of 80 and a standard deviation of 30. SE=30/100=3. The 95% interval is 80±1.96×3, which is 74.12 to 85.88.

The interval is about the mean, not about single orders. "95%" describes the method: it captures the true mean in 95% of samples.

q.stem: In a sample of 900 sessions, 10% convert. Using z = 1.96, what is the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the conversion rate? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain: SE=0.10×0.90/900=0.01. The lower bound is 0.10−1.96×0.01=0.0804, which rounds to 0.080.

blocks.html:
Tests and p-values

A test starts from a null hypothesis, usually "no effect". The p-value is the chance of seeing data at least this extreme if the null is true. A small p-value, usually below 0.05, is evidence against the null.

  • Type I error: you see an effect that isn't there. Its rate is the threshold you chose, such as 5%.
  • Type II error: you miss an effect that is there. Power is the chance of not missing it, and it grows with the sample size and with the size of the effect.

Watch for. A p-value is not the probability that the null is true. "Significant" does not mean "large": with a huge sample, a tiny difference is significant. And "not significant" does not prove that there is no effect.

Four biases to name on sight

  • Selection bias: the sample leaves out part of the population. Survivorship bias is the case where only the ones that lasted are counted.
  • Confounding: a third factor drives both of the things you compare, so a correlation is not a cause.
  • Simpson's paradox: a trend in every subgroup reverses when the groups are pooled.
  • Regression to the mean: an extreme first measurement tends to be followed by a less extreme one.

q.stem: Select the true statements.

options.text: A 95% confidence interval gets narrower as the sample grows.
options.why: The standard error shrinks with the square root of the sample size.

options.text: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true.
options.why: It is the chance of data this extreme if the null is true, not the chance that the null is true.

options.text: Four times the sample size halves the standard error of the mean.
options.why: The standard error divides by the square root of n, and the square root of 4 is 2.

options.text: A 99% interval is wider than a 95% interval from the same data.
options.why: More confidence needs a larger multiplier: 2.576 in place of 1.96.

options.text: A result that is not significant proves that there is no effect.
options.why: The test may lack the power to detect the effect.

q.explain: Intervals and tests both run on the standard error. More data shrinks it, which narrows intervals and raises power.

blocks.title: Exact values with NormalDist
blocks.code:
from statistics import NormalDist

scores = NormalDist(mu=70, sigma=10)
print("share above 90:     ", round(1 - scores.cdf(90), 4))
print("share from 60 to 90:", round(scores.cdf(90) - scores.cdf(60), 4))

# 95% interval for a mean: 100 orders, mean 80, standard deviation 30
se = 30 / 100**0.5
z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)
print("z for 95%:", round(z, 3))
print("interval: ", round(80 - z * se, 2), "to", round(80 + z * se, 2))
blocks.note: The rule of thumb says 2.5% lies above 2 standard deviations. The exact value is 2.28%. When a question tells you to use the rule, use the rule.

items: z = (value - mean) / SD. 68% within 1, 95% within 2, 99.7% within 3.
SE of a mean = s/√n. SE of a proportion = √(p(1-p)/n).
95% interval = estimate ± 1.96 × SE.
p-value: the chance of data this extreme if there is no effect.
Name the bias: selection, confounding, Simpson's paradox, regression to the mean.

lessons.title: Overfitting, underfitting, and regularization
lessons.intro: The most common question in this module gives you a training score and a validation score, and asks what is wrong and what would help. Two numbers lead to one of two diagnoses.

blocks.html:
Read the two scores

Training scoreValidation scoreDiagnosis
GoodMuch worseOverfitting (high variance). The model memorized noise in the training data.
PoorAbout as poorUnderfitting (high bias). The model is too simple for the pattern.
GoodAbout as goodA sound fit.

The two errors trade off. A more complex model has less bias and more variance. The best model sits where the validation error is lowest.

What helps

Overfitting: reduce varianceUnderfitting: reduce bias
More training dataA more flexible model
A simpler model: shallower trees, fewer featuresBetter features, interactions, polynomial terms
Stronger regularizationWeaker regularization
Early stopping, dropoutLonger training
Averaging many models (bagging)Boosting

More data helps overfitting. It does not help underfitting.

q.stem: A decision tree scores 100% on the training set and 71% on the validation set. Select what is likely to help.

options.text: Limit the depth of the tree.
options.why: A shallower tree can't isolate single rows.

options.text: Add more training rows.
options.why: More data makes noise harder to memorize.

options.text: Let the tree grow deeper.
options.why: It already fits the training data perfectly. More depth adds nothing but variance.

options.text: Replace it with a random forest.
options.why: Averaging many different trees cuts variance.

options.text: Add polynomial features.
options.why: More features give the tree more ways to memorize. That is a fix for underfitting.

q.explain: A perfect training score with a much lower validation score is overfitting. Every fix makes the model simpler, averages it, or gives it more data.

blocks.html:
Regularization

Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients to the loss, so the model pays for complexity.

L1 (lasso)L2 (ridge)
PenaltyThe sum of |w|The sum of w2
EffectSets some coefficients to exactly zeroShrinks every coefficient, none to zero
Use it forFeature selection, sparse modelsStability, correlated features

A stronger penalty means smaller coefficients, more bias, and less variance. Standardize the features first, because the penalty treats every coefficient alike.

Watch for. scikit-learn names the strength in two ways. In Ridge and Lasso, a larger alpha is stronger. In LogisticRegression and SVC, a larger C is weaker, because C is 1 divided by the strength.

Limits on tree depth, early stopping, dropout, and row subsampling do the same job for other models.

q.stem: You change C from 0.1 to 100 in a LogisticRegression and refit. What do you expect?

options.text: Weaker regularization: the coefficients can grow, and the risk of overfitting rises.
options.why: C is the inverse of the strength, so a larger C is a weaker penalty.

options.text: Stronger regularization: the coefficients shrink toward zero.
options.why: That is what a smaller C does.

options.text: More coefficients become exactly zero.
options.why: Exact zeros come from an L1 penalty, and from making it stronger.

options.text: The optimizer takes larger steps.
options.why: C is not a learning rate.

q.explain: Read C as "how much the model is allowed to fit". Read alpha as "how much the model is held back".

q.stem: As you add training rows, the training error rises a little and the validation error falls. The two curves meet at a high error and stay flat. What does this show?

options.text: High bias. More data will not help much: the model needs more capacity or better features.
options.why: The curves have already met, so there is no gap left for more data to close.

options.text: High variance. More data will close the gap.
options.why: High variance shows as a wide gap between the curves, and here there is none.

options.text: Data leakage.
options.why: Leakage shows as a validation score that is too good, not as a high error.

options.text: A learning rate that is too high.
options.why: That shows as a loss that jumps around or grows during training.

q.explain: A learning curve answers the question "would more data help". A wide gap says yes. Two curves stuck together at a high error say no.

blocks.title: Watch a tree overfit
blocks.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=600, n_features=20, n_informative=4,
                           flip_y=0.25, random_state=4)
X_tr, X_va, y_tr, y_va = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=4)

print("depth  train  validation")
for depth in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, None]:
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=4).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    train, valid = tree.score(X_tr, y_tr), tree.score(X_va, y_va)
    print(f"{str(depth):>5}  {train:.2f}   {valid:.2f}")
blocks.note: Training accuracy climbs to 1.00 as the tree gets deeper. Validation accuracy peaks at a depth of 2 or 3 and then falls. The gap between the two columns is overfitting. The labels here are noisy on purpose (flip_y), which is what a deep tree ends up memorizing.

items: Good on training, poor on validation: overfitting. Poor on both: underfitting.
Overfitting: more data, a simpler model, more regularization, early stopping, averaging.
Underfitting: a richer model or better features, less regularization.
L1 sets coefficients to zero. L2 shrinks them. Scale the features first.
A larger alpha is stronger. A larger C is weaker.

lessons.title: Reading linear and logistic models
lessons.intro: Expect a question that hands you coefficients or a loss function and asks what they mean. This lesson covers how to read a linear model, how to read a logistic model, and the three losses the test likes.

blocks.html:
Linear regression

y^=b0+b1x1+b2x2+… Each coefficient is the change in the prediction when its feature rises by one unit and the others stay fixed. The fit minimizes the squared error.

R2=1−SSESST is the share of the variance that the model explains. 1 is perfect, and 0 is no better than predicting the mean. On new data it can be negative.

Watch for. A bigger coefficient is not a more important feature unless the features share a scale. Standardize before you compare sizes. Highly correlated features make single coefficients unstable, even when the predictions are fine.

MSE, RMSE, and MAE

Worked example. The actual values are 3, 5, and 8. The predictions are 4, 5, and 6, so the errors are -1, 0, and 2.

MAE = (1+0+2)/3=1.000. MSE = (1+0+4)/3=1.667. RMSE = 1.667=1.291.

MSE and RMSEMAE
Large errorsPunished heavily, because they are squaredCounted in proportion
OutliersSensitiveRobust
Best constant predictionThe meanThe median

RMSE is in the units of the target, and it is never smaller than MAE.

q.stem: A model predicts 10, 20, and 30. The actual values are 12, 20, and 24. What is the RMSE? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain:
The errors are 2, 0, and -6. Their squares add up to 40, so the MSE is 40/3=13.333 and the RMSE is 13.333=3.651.

The MAE is 2.667. One large miss pulls the RMSE well above it.

blocks.html:
Logistic regression

The model adds up a score z=b0+b1x1+… and squashes it into a probability with the sigmoid:

p=11+e−z

The score z is the log of the odds, lnp1−p. So a coefficient acts on the log-odds, and eb is the factor by which the odds change when the feature rises by one unit. A coefficient of 0.69 doubles the odds. A negative coefficient lowers them.

Worked example. With b0=−1 and b1=0.5, a case with x=4 has z=1 and p=1/(1+e−1)=0.731. Each extra unit of x multiplies the odds by e0.5=1.649.

Values worth knowing: the sigmoid of 0 is 0.5, of 1 is 0.731, and of 2 is 0.881. The boundary p=0.5 is where z=0, which is a straight line in the features.

Log loss

Log loss, also called cross-entropy, scores the probabilities and not only the labels. For one case it is minus the log of the probability the model gave to what happened. The model's loss is the average over the cases.

Worked example. Three cases, with the probability the model gave to the true class: 0.9, 0.8, and 0.3.

−ln0.9=0.105, −ln0.8=0.223, and −ln0.3=1.204. The log loss is their mean, 0.511.

A confident right answer costs almost nothing. A confident wrong answer costs a lot. Always answering 0.5 costs ln2=0.693 per case.

q.stem: A classifier gives the positive class a probability of 0.8 for one case and 0.4 for another. The first case is positive and the second is negative. What is the log loss, using natural logs? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain:
Use the probability given to what happened: 0.8 for the first case, and 1−0.4=0.6 for the second.

−ln0.8−ln0.62=0.223+0.5112=0.367

q.stem: A logistic regression for loan default has a coefficient of 1.1 on "missed a payment last year" (0 or 1) and -0.4 on income, where income is standardized. Select the correct readings.

options.text: A missed payment multiplies the odds of default by about 3.
options.why: e to the power 1.1 is 3.0.

options.text: A missed payment raises the probability of default by 1.1.
options.why: Coefficients act on the log-odds. A probability can't rise by more than 1.

options.text: Higher income goes with lower odds of default.
options.why: The coefficient is negative.

options.text: One standard deviation more income multiplies the odds by about 0.67.
options.why: e to the power -0.4 is 0.67.

options.text: Nobody without a missed payment can get a predicted probability above 0.5.
options.why: The intercept and income also move the score, so the model can still predict above 0.5.

q.explain: Exponentiate a coefficient to get the factor on the odds. A factor above 1 raises the odds, and a factor below 1 lowers them.

blocks.title: Sigmoid and log loss by hand
blocks.code:
from math import exp, log

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + exp(-z))

# a logistic model: z = -1 + 0.5 * x
for x in [0, 2, 4, 6]:
    print(f"x = {x}:  p = {sigmoid(-1 + 0.5 * x):.3f}")
print("each extra unit of x multiplies the odds by", round(exp(0.5), 3))

# log loss for pairs of (true label, predicted probability of 1)
cases = [(1, 0.9), (0, 0.2), (1, 0.3)]
losses = [-log(p if y == 1 else 1 - p) for y, p in cases]
print("losses:", [round(v, 3) for v in losses])
print("log loss (their mean):", round(sum(losses) / len(losses), 3))
blocks.note: Change the last case to (1, 0.01) and run it again. One confident wrong answer dominates the mean.

items: A linear coefficient is the change in the prediction per unit.
A logistic coefficient is the change in the log-odds per unit, and e^b is the factor on the odds.
MSE punishes big misses and follows the mean. MAE is robust and follows the median.
Log loss = minus the log of the probability given to what happened, averaged.

lessons.title: Trees, forests, and boosting
lessons.intro: Tree models do most of the work in the coding tasks, and the quiz likes to ask how a random forest differs from gradient boosting.

blocks.html:
One tree

A tree splits the data on one feature at a time, and it picks the split that makes the two groups purest. A leaf predicts its majority class, or its mean for regression.

Purity for classes is usually measured by Gini impurity: 1−∑pi2, where pi is the share of each class in the node. A pure node scores 0, and an even two-class split scores 0.5.

Worked example. A node is 80% positive and 20% negative. Its Gini impurity is 1−(0.82+0.22)=0.32.

  • It needs no scaling: a split depends only on the order of the values.
  • It captures non-linear effects and interactions without help.
  • It can't extrapolate: outside the training range, the prediction is flat.
  • A deep tree memorizes the training data, and a small change in the data can change the whole tree.

Control it with max_depth, min_samples_leaf, and min_samples_split.

q.stem: A node holds 30 positive and 10 negative cases. What is its Gini impurity? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain: The shares are 0.75 and 0.25. 1−(0.752+0.252)=1−0.625=0.375.

blocks.html:
Random forest and gradient boosting

Both combine many trees. They do it in opposite ways.

Random forestGradient boosting
How the trees are builtIndependently, so in parallel. Each sees a bootstrap sample of the rows, and a random subset of the features at each split.One after another. Each new tree fits the errors of the trees so far.
Each tree isDeep, with low biasShallow and weak
Mainly reducesVariance, by averagingBias, step by step
Adding treesSafe. The gain flattens out.Can overfit. Stop when validation stops improving.
Noisy labelsRobustSensitive, because it keeps chasing the errors
Main settingsn_estimators, max_features, min_samples_leaflearning_rate, n_estimators, max_depth

In boosting, the learning rate scales each tree's contribution. A smaller learning rate needs more trees, and it usually generalizes better. In a forest, the rows a tree did not see (its out-of-bag rows) give a free validation score.

q.stem: A gradient boosting model's validation loss falls for the first 300 trees and rises after that. Its training loss is still falling at 1,000 trees. What should you do?

options.text: Keep about 300 trees, which is early stopping.
options.why: Past that point the new trees fit noise in the training data.

options.text: Add trees until the training loss stops falling.
options.why: Training loss keeps falling as the model memorizes. Validation loss is the one to watch.

options.text: Raise the learning rate.
options.why: Larger steps reach the overfitting point sooner.

options.text: Make each tree deeper.
options.why: Deeper trees add capacity, which makes the overfitting worse.

q.explain: Boosting can overfit because every new tree chases what is left of the training error. A validation set tells you where to stop.

q.stem: Which change makes the trees in a random forest less alike, so that averaging them helps more?

options.text: Consider fewer features at each split.
options.why: Each tree is pushed toward different splits, so their errors are less correlated.

options.text: Train every tree on the same rows.
options.why: Identical data gives near-identical trees, and averaging copies changes nothing.

options.text: Standardize the features.
options.why: Scaling doesn't change the splits a tree picks.

options.text: Grow fewer trees.
options.why: The number of trees doesn't change how alike they are.

q.explain: Averaging only helps when the models disagree. A forest forces disagreement with random rows and random features.

blocks.html:
Feature importance

Impurity-based importance is quick, but it is measured on the training data and it favors features with many distinct values. Permutation importance on validation data is more trustworthy. Correlated features split their importance between them.

blocks.title: One tree, a forest, and boosting
blocks.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=800, n_features=20, n_informative=10,
                           flip_y=0.1, random_state=5)
X_tr, X_va, y_tr, y_va = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=5)

models = {
    "one deep tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=5),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=5),
    "boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=5),
}
print("model           train  validation")
for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    train, valid = model.score(X_tr, y_tr), model.score(X_va, y_va)
    print(f"{name:<15} {train:.2f}   {valid:.2f}")
blocks.note: The single tree and the forest both fit the training data perfectly, but the forest scores much better on validation, because it averages 100 different trees. Set n_estimators=5 for the forest and run it again to see part of that gain disappear.

items: A tree needs no scaling, finds interactions, and overfits when deep.
Gini = 1 minus the sum of the squared class shares. Zero is pure.
Forest: deep trees on random rows and features, averaged. Cuts variance. Parallel.
Boosting: shallow trees in sequence, each fixing the errors so far. Cuts bias. Can overfit.
A smaller learning rate needs more trees. Stop when validation stops improving.

lessons.title: The other models, in brief
lessons.intro: You don't need the math of these models for the test. You need two or three facts about each: what it assumes, what it is sensitive to, and which setting controls how hard it fits.

blocks.html:
k-nearest neighbors

  • It predicts from the k closest training points: a vote for classes, an average for numbers.
  • There is no training step. Prediction is the slow part, because it searches the stored data.
  • A small k overfits, and a large k underfits. With k=1, training accuracy is 100%.
  • It runs on distances, so scale the features. Many irrelevant features drown the useful distances.

Naive Bayes

  • It applies Bayes' rule and assumes that the features are independent of each other within each class.
  • It is fast and copes with many features and little data, which is why it suits text.
  • Correlated features count the same evidence twice, so its probabilities are overconfident.
  • A value never seen with a class gives a zero probability unless you smooth the counts.

q.stem: In a k-nearest neighbors classifier, you move from k = 1 to k = 25. What do you expect?

options.text: Training accuracy drops from 100%, and the decision boundary gets smoother.
options.why: Each prediction now averages over 25 neighbors, so single noisy points lose their influence.

options.text: Training accuracy stays at 100%.
options.why: That holds only for k = 1, where every training point is its own nearest neighbor.

options.text: The model is more likely to overfit.
options.why: A larger k smooths the model. Overfitting is the risk at a small k.

options.text: The scale of the features stops mattering.
options.why: Distances depend on scale at any k.

q.explain: k is the complexity setting, and it runs backwards: a smaller k is a more flexible model.

blocks.html:
Support vector machines

  • An SVM looks for the boundary with the widest margin between the classes. Only the points near the boundary, the support vectors, decide where it goes.
  • A kernel such as RBF lets the boundary curve.
  • C: a small value means a wide margin and more regularization. A large value fits the training points harder.
  • gamma in the RBF kernel: a large value gives each point a short reach, so the boundary wiggles and overfits.
  • Scale the features first.

PCA and k-means

Both are unsupervised: they never see the target.

  • PCA rotates the features onto uncorrelated directions, ordered by how much variance each one holds. Keep the first few to reduce the number of dimensions. Standardize first, and fit on the training rows only. A direction with little variance can still be predictive.
  • k-means groups points around k centers. You choose k in advance, often with an elbow plot. It is sensitive to scale and to where the centers start, and it finds round clusters.

Who needs scaling

Scale the featuresNo need
k-NN, SVM, k-means, PCADecision trees
Linear and logistic regression with a penaltyRandom forests, gradient boosting
Neural networksNaive Bayes

Anything built on distances, penalties, or gradient descent needs scaled features. Trees only look at the order of the values.

q.stem: Select the true statements.

options.text: An SVM with a very large gamma in the RBF kernel tends to overfit.
options.why: Each training point then shapes only its own small neighborhood, so the boundary follows the noise.

options.text: PCA chooses the directions that best predict the target.
options.why: PCA never sees the target. It chooses the directions with the most variance.

options.text: k-means needs the number of clusters before it starts.
options.why: k is an input. Methods such as the elbow plot help you choose it.

options.text: k-NN gets faster at prediction as the training set grows.
options.why: It searches the stored training points, so more data makes prediction slower.

options.text: Only the points nearest the boundary decide where an SVM puts it.
options.why: Those are the support vectors. Points far from the boundary can move without changing it.

q.explain: For each model, know what it assumes, what it is sensitive to, and which setting makes it fit harder.

blocks.title: k-NN with and without scaling
blocks.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
print("largest value in each of the first 5 features:", X.max(axis=0)[:5].round(1))

raw = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
scaled = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5))

raw_score = cross_val_score(raw, X, y, cv=5).mean()
scaled_score = cross_val_score(scaled, X, y, cv=5).mean()
print("k-NN on raw features:   ", round(raw_score, 3))
print("k-NN on scaled features:", round(scaled_score, 3))
blocks.note: The features sit on very different scales, so raw distances are driven by the largest ones. The scaler is inside the pipeline, so each fold fits it on its own training part.

items: k-NN: a small k overfits, a large k underfits. Scale first. Slow to predict.
Naive Bayes: assumes independent features. Fast, but overconfident.
SVM: widest margin. A large C or a large gamma fits harder. Scale first.
PCA: directions of most variance, with no target. Fit on the training rows only.
Distances, penalties, and gradients need scaling. Trees don't.

lessons.title: Metrics and thresholds
lessons.intro: At least one quiz question, and the whole of the model coding task, depend on reading the right metric. Everything starts from four counts.

blocks.html:
Four counts

Predicted positivePredicted negative
Actually positiveTrue positive (TP)False negative (FN)
Actually negativeFalse positive (FP)True negative (TN)
MetricFormulaIn words
PrecisionTPTP+FPOf the cases you flagged, how many are real
Recall (sensitivity)TPTP+FNOf the real cases, how many you caught
False positive rateFPFP+TNOf the negatives, how many you flagged
F12×P×RP+ROne number that is high only when both are
AccuracyTP+TNallThe share of all cases you got right

Worked example. Out of 1,000 cases: TP = 40, FP = 20, FN = 10, and TN = 930.

Precision = 40 / 60 = 0.667. Recall = 40 / 50 = 0.800. F1 = 2×0.667×0.8000.667+0.800=0.727. Accuracy = 0.970. False positive rate = 20 / 950 = 0.021.

q.stem: A model produces 72 true positives, 18 false positives, and 48 false negatives. What is its F1 score? Round your answer to three decimal places.
q.explain:
Precision is 72/90=0.8, and recall is 72/120=0.6.

F1=2×0.8×0.60.8+0.6=0.961.4=0.686

F1 sits below the plain average of 0.7, because the harmonic mean leans toward the lower number.

blocks.html:
The threshold

A classifier outputs a score, and the threshold turns the score into a label. Moving the threshold trades one error for the other.

  • Raise it: fewer cases are flagged. Recall falls or stays the same, and precision usually rises.
  • Lower it: more cases are flagged. Recall rises or stays the same, and precision usually falls.

Choose it from the costs. If a miss is expensive, as in screening for a disease, favor recall. If a false alarm is expensive, as in blocking a customer's card, favor precision.

ROC AUC

The ROC curve plots recall against the false positive rate at every threshold. The area under it, AUC, is the chance that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative. 0.5 is random, and 1 is perfect.

  • It needs no threshold, and it doesn't change if you rescale the scores without reordering them.
  • It measures ranking. It says nothing about whether the probabilities are right.
  • With rare positives it can look strong while precision is poor. Look at the precision-recall curve as well.

Imbalanced classes

With 1% positives, a model that always says "negative" is 99% accurate and useless. Report precision, recall, F1, or the area under the precision-recall curve. To do better, use class weights, resample the training rows only, tune the threshold, and stratify the splits.

q.stem: A fraud model catches too few frauds. The business can afford more manual reviews. Select the sensible moves.

options.text: Lower the decision threshold.
options.why: More cases are flagged, so more frauds are caught, at the price of more reviews.

options.text: Use recall as the main metric.
options.why: Recall is the share of frauds that are caught, which is the stated problem.

options.text: Raise the decision threshold.
options.why: That flags fewer cases, so even fewer frauds are caught.

options.text: Use class weights so that a missed fraud costs more in training.
options.why: The model then pays more attention to the rare class.

options.text: Judge the model on accuracy.
options.why: With rare fraud, accuracy is high even when every fraud is missed.

q.explain: "Catches too few" is a recall problem. The business has said that false alarms are affordable, so trade precision for recall.

q.stem: In a dataset with 1% positives, a model has a ROC AUC of 0.95. Which statement is safe?

options.text: It ranks positives above negatives well, but its precision at a useful recall may still be low.
options.why: With 99 negatives for each positive, even a small false positive rate yields many false alarms.

options.text: About 95% of the cases it flags are positive.
options.why: That would be precision. AUC doesn't give it.

options.text: It classifies 95% of cases correctly.
options.why: That would be accuracy, and accuracy depends on the threshold.

options.text: Its predicted probabilities are well calibrated.
options.why: AUC only looks at the order of the scores.

q.explain: AUC is about ranking. To know what happens at a working threshold, compute precision and recall there.

blocks.title: Move the threshold
blocks.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4000, weights=[0.9], flip_y=0.02,
                           random_state=5)
X_tr, X_va, y_tr, y_va = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=5)

proba = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_va)[:, 1]
auc = roc_auc_score(y_va, proba)
print("ROC AUC:", round(auc, 3), "(one number for every threshold)")

print("threshold  flagged  precision  recall")
for t in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]:
    pred = (proba >= t).astype(int)
    p = precision_score(y_va, pred, zero_division=0)
    r = recall_score(y_va, pred)
    print(f"   {t:.1f}      {pred.sum():4d}     {p:.2f}      {r:.2f}")
blocks.note: As the threshold rises, fewer cases are flagged, recall falls, and precision climbs. This loop is also the tool for the model task when it sets a precision bar: pick the lowest threshold that clears the bar on validation data.

items: Precision: of the flagged, how many are real. Recall: of the real, how many you caught.
A higher threshold lowers recall and usually raises precision.
ROC AUC measures ranking. It has no threshold and says nothing about calibration.
With rare positives, skip accuracy.

lessons.title: Validation, leakage, and feature preparation
lessons.intro: These ideas decide whether a score can be trusted. They appear as quiz questions, and they are the whole point of the data processing task.

blocks.html:
Three jobs for your data

  • Training set: fit the model.
  • Validation set: choose between models and settings.
  • Test set: report the result once, at the end. If you tune on it, its score turns optimistic.

Cross-validation reuses the training data. Split it into k folds, validate on each fold in turn while you train on the rest, and average the scores. Every row is used for validation exactly once.

SituationSplit to use
Imbalanced classesStratified k-fold, which keeps the class shares in every fold
Several rows per customer, patient, or deviceGroup k-fold, which keeps each group in one fold
Data ordered in timeTrain on the past, validate on the future
Tuning and reporting from the same dataNested cross-validation

Grid search tries every combination of settings. Random search samples them, which covers a large space with fewer fits. GridSearchCV refits the best settings on all the training data when it finishes.

q.stem: You have three years of daily sales and want to forecast next month. Which validation fits?

options.text: Train on earlier dates and validate on later dates.
options.why: It matches how the model will be used: predicting a future that it has not seen.

options.text: Shuffled 5-fold cross-validation.
options.why: Shuffling puts future days in the training folds, so the model learns from the future.

options.text: Stratified 5-fold on the sales figure.
options.why: Stratifying balances classes. It does nothing about the order in time.

options.text: Leave-one-out cross-validation.
options.why: Each held-out day would be surrounded by its neighbors in the training data.

q.explain: Split the way the model will be used. For a forecast, that means the validation data comes after the training data.

blocks.html:
Leakage

Leakage means the model learned from something it won't have when it predicts for real. The score looks great and then collapses in use. It has three common forms:

  • Preprocessing fitted on all the rows. A scaler, imputer, encoder, feature selector, or PCA fitted before the split has seen the test rows.
  • Features from the future or from the target. "Refund issued" can't be used to predict whether an order is returned.
  • The same entity on both sides. Duplicate rows, or one customer's rows split between train and test.

Split first. Fit every transformer on the training rows only. Then transform both sets with it.

scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)   # learn from the training rows
X_train_s = scaler.transform(X_train)
X_test_s = scaler.transform(X_test)      # reuse it, never refit

A scikit-learn Pipeline inside cross-validation does this for every fold.

q.stem: Select the steps that leak.

options.text: Picking the 20 features most correlated with the target on all the rows, then cross-validating a model on those features.
options.why: The selection has already seen the validation rows of every fold.

options.text: Using a customer's total spend over the whole year to predict whether they churn in March.
options.why: Spend after March is information from the future.

options.text: Fitting a one-hot encoder on the training rows and applying it to the test rows.
options.why: That is the correct order: fit on train, transform test.

options.text: Filling missing values in the test set with the median from the training set.
options.why: The statistic comes from the training rows only, as it should.

options.text: Removing exact duplicate rows before you split.
options.why: That prevents leakage: a duplicate can no longer land on both sides.

q.explain: Ask of every step: did anything here use rows, or facts, that the model won't have at prediction time?

blocks.html:
Feature preparation facts

StepWhat to remember
Missing valuesMedian for skewed numbers, most frequent value for categories. Add a 0/1 "was missing" flag when the gap itself may carry signal.
EncodingOne-hot for categories with no order. Ordinal for ranks such as low, medium, high. For a category that first appears at prediction time, handle_unknown="ignore" gives all zeros.
ScalingStandardize to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, or min-max to the range 0 to 1.
Outliers and skewCap at fences such as Q1 - 1.5 IQR and Q3 + 1.5 IQR. Log-transform right-skewed amounts.

Every median, mean, category list, and fence comes from the training rows.

q.stem: Income is strongly right-skewed, with a few very large values. You are fitting a linear model. What is the usual first step for this feature?

options.text: Log-transform it, for example with log1p.
options.why: The log pulls in the long right tail, so a few huge incomes no longer dominate the fit.

options.text: One-hot encode it.
options.why: One-hot encoding is for categories. Income is a number.

options.text: Leave it, because linear models are not affected by skew.
options.why: A few extreme values can dominate a least-squares fit.

options.text: Min-max scale it with the minimum and maximum of the test set.
options.why: The statistics for a transform must come from the training rows.

q.explain: For right-skewed amounts such as income, price, or counts, a log transform is the standard move. Trees don't need it, but linear and distance-based models benefit.

blocks.title: A leak you can measure
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
X = rng.normal(size=(100, 2000))      # 2,000 features of pure noise
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=100)      # labels that have nothing to do with X

# wrong: pick the best 20 features using every row, then cross-validate
X_leaky = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit_transform(X, y)
leaky = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_leaky, y, cv=5).mean()

# right: the selection is inside the pipeline, so each fold picks its own features
pipe = make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20), LogisticRegression())
honest = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5).mean()

print("selection outside cross-validation:", round(leaky, 2))
print("selection inside the pipeline:     ", round(honest, 2))
blocks.note: The data is noise, so an honest score is close to 0.5. Selecting the features on all the rows first makes noise look like signal. Change the seed in default_rng and run it again: the honest score wobbles around 0.5, and the leaky one stays high.

items: Train to fit, validation to choose, test to report once.
Split first. Fit every transformer on the training rows only.
A Pipeline inside cross-validation keeps each fold clean.
Grouped rows: group k-fold. Time order: train on the past.
A score that looks too good is a leak until you have ruled it out.

lessons.title: Neural networks and gradient descent
lessons.intro: The test stays at fundamentals here: what activation functions do, which output layer goes with which loss, and how to read a training run that goes wrong.

blocks.html:
Activations

Each unit computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through an activation function. Without a non-linear activation, any number of layers collapses into one linear model.

FunctionOutputWhere it goes
ReLU: max(0,z)0 and upHidden layers, by default. It is cheap, and its gradient doesn't fade for positive inputs.
Sigmoid0 to 1The output for a yes/no target. In deep hidden layers it saturates, and the gradients vanish.
Tanh-1 to 1Hidden layers in older and recurrent networks. It is centered on zero, but it saturates too.
SoftmaxProbabilities that add up to 1The output for several classes.

Output layer and loss

TaskOutput activationLoss
RegressionLinear (none)MSE, or MAE
Two classesSigmoidBinary cross-entropy (log loss)
Several classesSoftmaxCategorical cross-entropy

q.stem: You build a network that sorts images into 10 classes. Which output layer and loss go together?

options.text: Softmax with categorical cross-entropy.
options.why: Softmax gives one probability for each class, and cross-entropy is its matching loss.

options.text: Sigmoid with mean squared error.
options.why: One sigmoid gives a single yes/no probability, and squared error is a regression loss.

options.text: ReLU with cross-entropy.
options.why: ReLU outputs are not probabilities: they can be 0, or far above 1.

options.text: Linear with hinge loss.
options.why: That is the support vector machine setup, which gives no probabilities.

q.explain: Match the output to the target: a number needs a linear output, a yes/no target needs a sigmoid, and one of several classes needs softmax.

blocks.html:
Gradient descent

Training repeats one move: work out the gradient of the loss for every weight, by backpropagation, and step against it.

w←w−η×gradient

η is the learning rate. Too high, and the steps overshoot, so the loss jumps around or grows. Too low, and training crawls.

Worked example. The loss is L(w)=(w−3)2, so the gradient is 2(w−3). At w=0 the gradient is -6. With a learning rate of 0.1, the step gives w=0−0.1×(−6)=0.6, which is closer to the minimum at 3.

  • A batch is the set of rows used for one step. Mini-batches, such as 32 rows, are the norm: noisy, but fast.
  • An epoch is one pass over all the training rows.
  • Scale the inputs. Otherwise the loss surface is steep in some directions and flat in others.
  • Optimizers such as Adam adapt the step size for each weight.

q.stem: The loss is L(w) = (w - 4)², and you start at w = 1 with a learning rate of 0.25. What is w after one step of gradient descent?
q.explain:
The gradient is 2(w−4)=2×(1−4)=−6.

w=1−0.25×(−6)=2.5

blocks.html:
When training goes wrong

What you seeLikely causeWhat to try
Training loss jumps around or growsThe learning rate is too high, or the inputs are not scaledLower the rate, scale the inputs, clip the gradients
Training loss barely movesThe learning rate is too low, or the gradients vanishRaise the rate, use ReLU, use batch normalization
Training loss falls, validation loss risesOverfittingEarly stopping, dropout, weight decay, more data
Every unit in a layer learns the same thingAll the weights started at the same valueRandom initialization
  • Dropout switches off random units during training. It is off at prediction time.
  • Weight decay is an L2 penalty on the weights.
  • Vanishing gradients: in a deep stack of sigmoid or tanh layers, the gradient shrinks at each layer, so the early layers stop learning. ReLU helps.

q.stem: After epoch 12, the training loss keeps falling and the validation loss starts to rise. Select the reasonable responses.

options.text: Keep the weights from about epoch 12.
options.why: That is early stopping: the best validation loss marks the point to keep.

options.text: Add dropout.
options.why: Dropout stops units from relying on each other, which limits memorizing.

options.text: Train for more epochs.
options.why: The gap is already widening. More epochs widen it further.

options.text: Add weight decay.
options.why: An L2 penalty keeps the weights small, which limits how closely the network can fit noise.

options.text: Add more layers.
options.why: More capacity makes overfitting worse.

q.explain: A falling training loss with a rising validation loss is the neural network version of overfitting. The fixes are the same family as before: stop earlier, regularize, or get more data.

blocks.title: Four learning rates
blocks.note: The minimum is at w = 3. With 0.01 the steps crawl: after six of them, w has barely left 0. With 0.3 they settle on 3. With 0.9 they overshoot from side to side but still close in. With 1.1 every step lands farther away, and the loss grows: that is divergence.

items: No non-linear activation, no depth: the network is one linear model.
Hidden layers: ReLU. Two classes: sigmoid with cross-entropy. Several classes: softmax with cross-entropy. A number: linear with MSE.
One step: w becomes w minus the learning rate times the gradient.
Too high a rate diverges. Too low a rate crawls.
Validation loss rising while training loss falls: stop early, add dropout or weight decay.
